opus-5.5.text:
Look, I think people underrate this in both directions. On one hand, there's this comforting story in the West that China just can't do frontier AI because they don't have the secret sauce, the tacit knowledge of how to actually get a giant training run to converge, how to handle loss spikes, how to debug at the scale of tens of thousands of GPUs. And it's true that a lot of that knowledge is genuinely tacit. It lives in the heads of a few hundred people at a handful of labs. It's not in the papers.

But on the other hand, I think it's way more acquirable than people assume, for a couple of reasons.

First, China has a huge pool of very talented engineers, and a lot of the researchers at the top American labs are themselves Chinese nationals or have deep ties there. That's not a knock on those individuals. The vast majority are wonderful people doing great work. But it means the knowledge is flowing through networks that are very hard to wall off.

Second, and this is the thing I keep harping on, the security at these labs is just not where it needs to be. We're talking startup-level security against what will increasingly be nation-state-level espionage. If the CCP decides this is a top priority, and I think they will, they can steal the weights, but they can also steal the algorithmic secrets, the recipes, the internal docs, the Slack threads where people are debugging the run. You don't need to rediscover tacit knowledge if you can just read the postmortems.

Third, tacit knowledge is learnable by doing. You've seen Chinese labs put out models that are, frankly, surprisingly close to the frontier, often with a lot less compute. That tells you they're building up their own engineering muscle. Every time they do a big run, they learn the same painful lessons the American labs learned.

So my assessment is: the tacit knowledge gap is real today, it's maybe a year or so, but it's not a durable moat. The durable advantages we have are compute, the chips and the fabs and the power, and potentially the algorithmic lead, but only if we actually lock down the labs. If we don't, the tacit knowledge gap basically disappears, and then it comes down to who can build the bigger clusters faster. And China is very, very good at building things fast.

r001.rationale: The response says tacit knowledge is learnable through repeated training runs, where Chinese labs build engineering skill and learn the same lessons over time—framing it as an achievable engineering grind.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is actually one of the most underrated questions in the whole China debate, because people tend to collapse it into "can they get the chips" or "can they get the weights." And those matter. But the thing that actually makes a frontier training run work isn't written down anywhere. It's not in the papers. It's in the heads of maybe a few hundred people at the top labs.

So, think about what a big run actually involves. You've got tens of thousands of GPUs, and something is always breaking. You get loss spikes, you get weird divergences, and the question of whether you restart from a checkpoint or lower the learning rate or just ride it out, that's a judgment call. There's a whole folk knowledge around data mixtures, around how you tune your hyperparameters as you scale, around what the right ratio of this to that is. Mostly you learn it by having burned fifty million dollars doing it wrong once. The labs guard this stuff really jealously. They don't publish it anymore. That's the actual moat right now, far more than the algorithms, which mostly leak within a year or two anyway.

Now, does China have a shortfall there? I think yes, meaningfully. If you look at who's actually run a frontier-scale training run end to end, it's a very short list, and it's overwhelmingly concentrated in the US and a bit in the UK. China has very good researchers, a lot of them trained in the US, but the specific experience of pushing a run at the absolute frontier is scarcer there.

But I'd be careful about getting complacent for three reasons. One, tacit knowledge diffuses through people, and people move. Every year there are researchers going back, there's the diaspora, there are joint ventures. Two, a lot of it is compressible once you know it's possible. The hardest part is often knowing a thing works at all. Once you know the destination, the path is a lot easier to find, and the open-source ecosystem has been giving away a lot of the map. And three, honestly, the state of security at the labs has been pretty poor. If you're a determined state actor, you don't need to rederive the tacit knowledge. You steal the internal docs, the Slack history, the postmortems. That's where the tacit knowledge gets partly codified. So the gap is real, it's maybe one to two years of hard-won experience, but it's not a durable gap unless we actually treat it like the national security asset it is. And right now we mostly don't.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the gap as real but temporary: know-how spreads through people, becomes easier to reproduce once its feasibility is known, and amounts to perhaps one to two years of hard-won experience. This frames acquisition as achievable through sustained engineering effort.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between knowing the basic recipe and being able to execute it. You can read the papers, you can know roughly what architecture to use, and you can acquire chips. But making a large training run work involves a lot of knowledge that isn’t written down: how to keep the cluster running, how to diagnose an instability, which experiments are worth doing, and which apparent problems you can safely ignore.

That’s a real advantage for the leading labs. But I wouldn’t assume it’s an enduring barrier for China. This knowledge lives in people, and people can move. A relatively small number of experienced engineers could save another team a lot of failed experiments. And Chinese teams can also develop that expertise themselves by doing progressively larger runs.

The key question is how quickly they can do that relative to how quickly the frontier moves. Reproducing something you know works is easier than discovering it in the first place. But if the leading labs keep moving to scales where new problems emerge, catching up requires more than copying yesterday’s recipe. So I’d treat tacit knowledge as a meaningful source of delay, rather than something that makes catching up impossible.

r001.rationale: The response says Chinese teams can build the expertise through progressively larger runs and treats tacit knowledge as a delay rather than an impossible barrier, framing acquisition as a tractable engineering effort.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different questions here. One is whether they can get the chips, and the other is whether they can make a large cluster work effectively. Getting the chips doesn’t automatically give you the ability to run a frontier training job. You need people who know how to diagnose failures, keep the network working, and figure out why a run is behaving strangely. A lot of that knowledge comes from actually doing it.

But I wouldn’t treat that as some permanent moat. Tacit knowledge is hard to transfer through a paper, but it can travel with people. And you can develop it yourself if you have enough compute to experiment and a strong engineering team. So the question is less, “Can China ever figure this out?” and more, “How much time and compute will it cost them to figure it out?”

That’s also why access to compute matters beyond the immediate training run. It gives you the opportunity to build the organization and accumulate that experience. If you constrain that access, you’re potentially slowing down both the models and the engineering capability behind them.

r001.rationale: The response says tacit knowledge is not a permanent moat and can be developed through experimentation with enough compute and a strong engineering team, framing the challenge as a matter of time and compute.
